w: L17 · Pregnancy and Lactation Hormonal support of pregnancy and the role of the placenta/corpus luteum Without a pregnancy the corpus luteum dies about 14 days after ovulation and its hormones crash. In a pregnancy, hCG from the embryo rescues it: the corpus luteum carries the first trimester, then the placenta takes over the hormones, with the fetus's help for estrogen. Know this Progesterone from the corpus luteum is the key hormone that prepares the endometrium for implantation (wider vessels, glycogen vacuoles). With no pregnancy, about 14 days after ovulation the corpus luteum regresses into the corpus albicans and estrogen and progesterone fall abruptly. hCG is made by the trophoblasts (the syncytiotrophoblasts), later the placenta, from about 8 days after ovulation. The corpus luteum doesn't make it; it responds to it. hCG rescues the corpus luteum: no regression, and more progesterone and estrogen. LH and FSH stay suppressed, so the cycle and periods stop. The lecture's summary: "hCG prevents the regression of corpus luteum, slows production of LH and FSH." A pregnancy test measures hCG: in urine or blood about 10 to 11 days after fertilization. It peaks at about 10 weeks, toward the end of the first trimester, then declines. hCG weakly stimulates the TSH receptor: a transient gestational hyperthyroidism. Estrogen raises TBG, so total T3 and T4 can double while free T3 and T4 barely rise. First trimester: the corpus luteum makes most of the progesterone and estrogen. The placenta starts developing shortly after implantation, is fully developed by the end of the first trimester, then takes over hormone production. The placenta exchanges gases and nutrients (oxygen, water, electrolytes and nutrients in; carbon dioxide and waste out, into the mother's blood), makes hormones, and protects the fetus while letting maternal antibodies through. It is not an absolute barrier: some drugs and viruses cross. The steroids start from the mother's cholesterol. The placenta makes progesterone on its own, but it lacks 17,20 desmolase, so estrogen needs the fetus: the fetal adrenal makes DHEA sulfate, the fetal liver 16-hydroxylates it, and the placenta's aromatase makes estriol. Estriol is the estrogen of pregnancy (estradiol is the cycle's, estrone menopause's). Because it needs a working fetal adrenal and liver, the mother's estriol reflects the health of the fetus. Human placental lactogen (hPL), also called human chorionic somatomammotropin, from the syncytiotrophoblasts: breast growth, and anti-insulin actions (lipolysis, breakdown of carbohydrates and proteins) that keep fuel flowing to the fetus. So pregnancy is insulin resistant and hyperinsulinemic, and some mothers get gestational diabetes, which the lecture called multifactorial. Relaxin, from the corpus luteum (under hCG) and the placenta, inhibits myometrial contractions ("the last thing we want is a preterm delivery"), relaxes the pelvic ligaments and softens the cervix. hCG Trophoblasts, then the placenta Rescues the corpus luteum; the pregnancy test Progesterone Corpus luteum, then the placenta on its own Readies the endometrium; relaxes the myometrium Estriol Placenta, with the fetal adrenal and liver Pregnancy's estrogen; reflects fetal health hPL Syncytiotrophoblasts (placenta) Breast growth; opposes insulin Relaxin Corpus luteum and placenta Keeps the uterus quiet; softens the cervix Watch for: hCG is made by the trophoblasts and acts on the corpus luteum; it doesn't turn it into the corpus albicans. Don't flip the steroids: progesterone alone, estrogen with the fetus, and the 16-hydroxylation is the fetal liver, not the kidney. The placenta isn't complete at implantation. hPL is not hCG, and it isn't made by the cytotrophoblasts (the nurse cells). Insulin rises in pregnancy. Relaxin quiets the uterus. The placenta doesn't make oxytocin. The lecture credits hCG itself with lowering LH and FSH; textbooks credit the high estrogen and progesterone it keeps up. No question depends on which. Hormonal changes associated with delivery and the postpartum period Labor starts when stretch and a shift in hormones turn a quiet uterus into a contracting one. Oxytocin is "the big one," and it keeps working after the birth to limit bleeding; delivering the placenta drops progesterone, which lets milk production start. Know this Parturition comes about 40 weeks after the onset of the last menstrual period, not 40 weeks after fertilization. Distention of the uterus by the growing fetus is a trigger: the stretch sets off the hormonal signals. The uterus upregulates its receptors for PGF2 alpha and oxytocin. The uterus becomes more sensitive to estrogen and less to progesterone: the estrogen-to-progesterone ratio rises and the myometrium shifts to contracting. Estrogen contracts, progesterone relaxes. Uterine prostaglandins rise and raise intracellular calcium, so contractions get stronger. PGF2 alpha: contraction. PGE2: softens and thins the cervix. Oxytocin from the mother's posterior pituitary (made in the hypothalamus) is "the big one": it drives the contractions and synergizes with the prostaglandins, by positive feedback (contractions bring more oxytocin). Relaxin may help relax and thin the cervix at term. After delivery, oxytocin keeps the uterus contracting once the placenta is out, which prevents excessive bleeding: "oxytocin has a role both during active delivery and post-delivery." Delivering the placenta makes progesterone fall, which takes the brake off prolactin: full milk production begins. Postpartum, suckling keeps prolactin high and releases oxytocin for letdown, and the high prolactin inhibits GnRH, so periods often stay away while breastfeeding. Uterine stretch Trigger for the hormonal signals Rising estrogen-to-progesterone ratio Myometrium shifts to contracting PGF2 alpha Contraction (its receptors go up) PGE2 Softens and thins the cervix Oxytocin (posterior pituitary) Contractions, positive feedback; limits bleeding after delivery Progesterone falls (placenta out) Frees prolactin to make milk Watch for: "40 weeks after fertilization" is false: the count starts at the last menstrual period, about two weeks earlier. The PGF2 alpha and oxytocin receptors go up, not down. The ratio rises toward estrogen, which favors contraction. Don't swap the prostaglandins: PGE2 is the cervix, PGF2 alpha the contraction. After delivery oxytocin limits bleeding; it doesn't raise progesterone or rescue the corpus luteum. Prolactin vs. oxytocin Two pituitary hormones with two jobs in the breast: "Prolactin sets the stage and creates all the milk products. Oxytocin is going to stimulate milk letdown." Prolactin makes the milk; oxytocin squeezes it out. Know this Prolactin = milk production. Oxytocin = milk letdown (ejection). A choice that swaps them is the obvious trap. Prolactin comes from the anterior pituitary and is tonically inhibited by dopamine from the hypothalamus. Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary into the blood. Prolactin, with cortisol, raises the milk enzymes during pregnancy, and after delivery it drives full milk production in the alveoli. Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells around each alveolus, which squeezes the milk out. It doesn't make milk or milk enzymes. During pregnancy prolactin rises, especially late, but is antagonized by progesterone, so full milk waits for delivery. Prolactin also inhibits GnRH: LH, FSH and the sex steroids fall, and periods stop. Oxytocin also drives labor contractions (positive feedback) and limits bleeding after delivery. Suckling turns both on: it lowers dopamine (so prolactin rises) and releases oxytocin. Source Anterior pituitary Hypothalamus; released from the posterior pituitary Control Dopamine holds it down; suckling lowers dopamine Suckling releases it In the breast Milk enzymes and milk production Myoepithelial cells contract: letdown Pregnancy and labor Rises, but progesterone antagonizes it Labor contractions, positive feedback After delivery Full milk; inhibits GnRH Letdown; limits uterine bleeding Watch for: Oxytocin lets milk down by contracting the myoepithelial cells, not by making the alveolar cells produce milk enzymes. The brake on prolactin is dopamine, not oxytocin or GnRH. Progesterone doesn't make milk. Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary or the placenta. Neuroendocrine effects of suckling Suckling is a reflex from the nipple to the hypothalamus. It takes the dopamine brake off prolactin and releases oxytocin, so one stimulus both makes the milk and lets it down, and the high prolactin also shuts the cycle down. On this slide Dr. Madison said: "mainly focus on this side of things. Dopamine being important." Know this At baseline the hypothalamus releases dopamine all the time, "a potent inhibitor of prolactin release from the anterior pituitary." Without a baby to feed, prolactin stays low. Suckling decreases dopamine. The lecture adds that the baby's sounds and sight and the emotions of delivery can lower it too. With dopamine down, the anterior pituitary releases prolactin, and prolactin releasing factor pushes it higher. Low dopamine means high prolactin. Prolactin drives full milk production in the alveoli. Suckling also makes the hypothalamus produce oxytocin, which is released from the posterior pituitary into the blood. Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells: milk letdown. "One thing that I want to highlight": prolactin inhibits GnRH. Less GnRH means less LH and FSH and lower sex steroids, so amenorrhea. That is why a breastfeeding mother's periods often stop, the same mechanism as hyperprolactinemia from any cause. This circuit turns on after delivery. Some prolactin is made in pregnancy, but progesterone holds it back. Watch for: Suckling lowers dopamine: a statement that it raises dopamine, or a choice blaming "high dopamine from suckling," is wrong. Prolactin, not oxytocin, inhibits GnRH. A breastfeeding mother's missing periods are not leftover hCG keeping her corpus luteum alive. The lecture says the baby's sounds and sight lower dopamine; physiology texts tie the baby's cry mainly to oxytocin and letdown. No question depends on which. Regulation of milk production and milk ejection The breast is built during pregnancy but kept from full milk production until delivery, because progesterone blocks prolactin. After delivery, making milk is prolactin's job and ejecting it is oxytocin's, and suckling keeps both going. Know this The high estrogen and progesterone of pregnancy (corpus luteum, then placenta) build the breast. Estrogen: ductal and lobular growth and ductal branching, and more fat. Breast fat expresses aromatase, so the breast makes estrogen locally. Progesterone: increases the number of alveoli, the milk-producing structures. Prolactin (rising, especially late) and cortisol: both increase the milk enzymes. Human placental lactogen also helps breast tissue grow. "What you should know": progesterone antagonizes prolactin, especially locally in the breast, so there may be a little milk but no full milk production until after delivery. Delivering the placenta makes progesterone fall; the brake comes off, and prolactin drives full milk production in the alveoli. Production stays on because suckling keeps dopamine low, so prolactin stays high, with prolactin releasing factor adding to it. Ejection (letdown): suckling releases oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, which contracts the myoepithelial cells around each alveolus and squeezes the milk out. Estrogen Ducts, branching, fat Not on the slide Progesterone More alveoli; antagonizes prolactin Falls when the placenta is delivered Prolactin (with cortisol) Raises the milk enzymes, but held back Full milk production Oxytocin Labor contractions Milk letdown Dopamine Tonically inhibits prolactin Suckling lowers it Watch for: Progesterone, not estrogen or prolactin, adds the alveoli; estrogen, not progesterone, grows and branches the ducts. Cortisol raises the milk enzymes, it doesn't lower them. Full milk waits for delivery because placental progesterone antagonizes prolactin, not because the alveoli are missing, the placenta makes dopamine, or oxytocin blocks prolactin. The lecture and slide name only progesterone as prolactin's antagonist in pregnancy (textbooks add estrogen); the hub's questions use progesterone. Key terms hCG Human chorionic gonadotropin, made by the trophoblasts from about 8 days after ovulation. It rescues the corpus luteum, so progesterone and estrogen stay high and LH and FSH stay low, and it is what a pregnancy test measures (10 to 11 days after fertilization; peak at about 10 weeks). progesterone The hormone that prepares the endometrium for implantation and relaxes the myometrium; made by the corpus luteum through the first trimester, then by the placenta on its own. In the breast it adds alveoli and antagonizes prolactin until it falls at delivery. prolactin The anterior pituitary hormone of milk production, tonically inhibited by dopamine and released when suckling lowers dopamine. High prolactin inhibits GnRH, causing the amenorrhea of breastfeeding. oxytocin Made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary: it contracts the myoepithelial cells for milk letdown, drives labor contractions by positive feedback, and keeps the uterus contracting after delivery to limit bleeding. Not a placental hormone. L18 · Estrogens and Androgens Major actions of estrogens, progestins, and androgens The sex steroids come from cholesterol, ride on SHBG and act on nuclear receptors, so their effects take time. Testosterone acts mostly as DHT or becomes estradiol; estrogen builds the female body, the uterine lining and bone, and raises clotting; progesterone matures the endometrium. Know this Synthesis: cholesterol, in several steps, to DHEA (dehydroepiandrosterone), then androstenedione, then testosterone. Testosterone's two fates: 5-alpha-reductase reduces it to DHT, the active form ("Dihydrotestosterone is the active testosterone"), and aromatase turns it into estradiol. How they act: lipophilic, carried on SHBG (the corticosteroids ride CBG); only the free hormone enters the cell, binds its nuclear receptor (DHT is the main androgen receptor ligand), and the complex changes gene expression, so the effect takes time. Testosterone's effects: male differentiation and puberty; sperm formation; more red blood cells; retention of water and electrolytes; lower HDL; more protein synthesis and muscle; thicker skin; libido; and it lowers plasma CBG, TBG, SHBG and transferrin. Growth: DHT stimulates growth and estradiol closes the epiphyses. A man without aromatase makes no estradiol and grows very tall with weak, osteoporotic bones; the treatment is estradiol. The natural estrogens: estradiol (E2) from the ovary; estrone (E1) and estriol (E3) from the liver and peripheral tissues, which go out in the bile and are reabsorbed from the gut (enterohepatic recirculation). Oral estrogens act more on the liver, including a rise in clotting factors. In the blood estrogen rides SHBG and albumin, and the free hormone binds the estrogen receptor. Estrogen's effects: female maturation (vagina, uterus, secondary sex traits); growth of the uterine muscle and lining; raises HDL and triglycerides; maintains the skin and blood vessels (some teens get the pill for bad skin); antagonizes PTH-driven bone resorption; raises clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lowers antithrombin III. Progesterone (adrenal cortex, corpus luteum, placenta, testes): the action he stressed is maturation of the endometrium. Progestin drugs activate its receptor and suppress FSH (next item). HDL Lowers it Raises it (and triglycerides) Growth DHT stimulates growth Estradiol closes the epiphyses Blood More red blood cells More clotting factors, less antithrombin III Fluid Retains water and electrolytes Fluid retention Watch for: DHEA is dehydroepiandrosterone, the precursor; his slide's table mislabels it "dihydrotestosterone," and he corrected it in class. Testosterone lowers the binding globulins and HDL, travels on SHBG (not CBG) and acts on a nuclear receptor (not a cell-surface one). A man without aromatase is tall, not short. Estrogen grows the uterine lining; it doesn't thin it. Two slides disagree on estrogen and LDL, so lean on HDL. The rest of his second estrogen-effects slide (ACTH, well-being, binding globulins, FSH and LH inhibition) he skipped: not needed. How hormonal contraceptives prevent pregnancy Hormonal contraception mostly works by stopping ovulation: a progestin, often with ethinyl estradiol, holds down FSH and LH. Women who can't take estrogen use a progestin alone. Emergency contraception is a big dose of a progestin (Plan B) or a progestin receptor blocker (ulipristal). Know this Progestins activate the progestin receptor, which suppresses FSH (and LH and estradiol), so there is no ovulation. The combined pill's estrogen is ethinyl estradiol, the semi-synthetic one. Levonorgestrel is the most common progestin in oral contraceptives. Women who can't take estrogen (a history or family history of thromboembolism, or breast or uterine cancer) avoid pills with ethinyl estradiol and take a progestin-only pill. His Case 3: of ethinyl estradiol, estradiol, levonorgestrel and estrone, the least estrogenic is levonorgestrel, a progestin. Dr. Madison's version (L17): the pill's estrogen blunts the LH surge, so there is no normal ovulation; it also thins the lining, and its progestin thickens the cervical mucus so sperm can't get into the uterus. High-dose estrogen prevents implantation (the lining proliferates but misses progesterone's preparation), and so do the IUD and progesterone receptor antagonists. Plan B is a high dose of levonorgestrel: within 72 hours, no prescription. Ulipristal (Ella) is a progestin receptor antagonist: up to 120 hours (5 days), prescription only. Same indication as Plan B. Mifepristone blocks the progestin and the glucocorticoid receptor, so it is contraindicated in Addison disease. Anti-progestins are avoided when pregnancy is wanted soon. Progestin cautions: hypertension (an adverse effect and a contraindication), lower HDL, and pregnancy wanted in the near future. What it is High-dose levonorgestrel, a progestin Progestin receptor antagonist Window Within 72 hours Up to 120 hours (5 days) Prescription Not needed Needed Watch for: Progestins activate the progestin receptor; blocking it is what the anti-progestins do (ulipristal, mifepristone). Plan B is levonorgestrel, not ethinyl estradiol, and not ulipristal at another strength. Its window is 72 hours, not 24. Progestins lower HDL. Thick cervical mucus is the progestin's doing. The pill's estrogen blunts the LH surge; it doesn't trigger an early one, raise prolactin or act like hCG. Dr. Madison skipped the methods that keep sperm and egg apart. Major drug classes that alter reproductive hormone signaling "The names will suggest to you how they work": each class supplies a hormone, blocks its receptor, or stops it from being made, so know what the target enzyme or receptor does. Learn the drugs his slides highlight in red (the table's "drugs to know"): "Pay attention to those drugs that I highlight in the slides, and you should be fine." Know this Androgens: testosterone, the standard (Schedule III; gels, a patch, a nasal gel, injections), and testosterone cypionate (Depo-Testosterone), the intramuscular depot, injected about once a week or once a month. Both are 1 to 1 androgenic to anabolic. DHEA (prasterone), the precursor, is sold over the counter, the one testosterone product that escapes Schedule III. GnRH analogs: goserelin (Zoladex), also leuprolide (Lupron). Natural GnRH comes in pulses; a long-acting analog stimulates without a pause, the pituitary cells switch off, and FSH, LH and testosterone fall. Mainly prostate cancer; also BPH, precocious puberty and chemical castration. Side effects are anti-sex-hormonal: impotence and gynecomastia. Estrogens: estradiol (patch, gel, injection) for replacement; ethinyl estradiol, semi-synthetic, for oral contraceptives; estrone, the main ingredient of Premarin (from pregnant mares), for menopause therapy. SERMs are tissue-selective because ER-alpha and ER-beta are expressed at different levels in different tissues: an agonist in one, an antagonist in another. Tamoxifen (Nolvadex): antagonist in the breast, agonist in the uterus; only for ER-positive breast cancer ("That is the only time you give tamoxifen"). Raloxifene (Evista): postmenopausal osteoporosis; no endometrial or breast stimulation. On his SERM table, uterine cell proliferation separates it from tamoxifen; both promote bone, and neither stimulates breast cells or inhibits ovulation. Clomiphene (Clomid): a weak agonist, strong antagonist that blocks estrogen's negative feedback, so the LH and FSH pulses grow and the ovary ovulates; it needs an intact hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. "Tamoxifen for breast cancer, raloxifene for osteoporosis, Clomid... to stimulate ovulation." Aromatase inhibitors: anastrozole (Arimidex), also letrozole and exemestane, block testosterone's conversion to estradiol, for breast cancer. Progestins and anti-progestins are the item above; the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors and androgen receptor antagonists the item below. Goserelin doesn't block a receptor or 5-alpha-reductase, and it doesn't mimic the pulses: it works by never pausing. Osteoporosis is raloxifene's use, not a GnRH analog's or clomiphene's. Premarin is estrone, for menopause; ethinyl estradiol is the pill's. Cypionate is no more anabolic than testosterone. Said not needed: the other androgen analogs on his table and the rarely used SERMs (toremifene, ospemifene, bazedoxifene, fulvestrant). Drugs that block androgen receptors or androgen metabolism "An anti-androgen either blocks testosterone at its receptor, prevents its activation to DHT, or shuts down its production." This item is the first two: the 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors stop testosterone from becoming DHT, and the androgen receptor antagonists compete with it at the receptor. The GnRH analogs, which shut down production, are in the item above. Know this Testosterone isn't very active until 5-alpha-reductase reduces it to DHT: its bioactivation. His Case 2: the enzyme that makes testosterone biologically active is 5-alpha-reductase (aromatase would make estradiol). 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors: finasteride (Proscar, Propecia) and dutasteride (Avodart). They block testosterone's conversion to DHT. Uses: BPH and alopecia. Proscar and Propecia are the same drug, finasteride: "the difference between Proscar and Propecia is the dose, the strength of the tablet," and the indication. Higher strength for BPH, lower strength for hair loss. Side effects: gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction. His Case 4, in the dental chair: a man on finasteride for hair loss with a lower libido and breast tenderness; the drug is blocking 5-alpha-reductase. Androgen receptor antagonists: flutamide (Eulexin) and bicalutamide (Casodex) (nilutamide and enzalutamide are on the slide too): competitive antagonism at the androgen receptor. Uses: prostate cancer in men and excess androgens in women. Side effects: GI disturbances (least with bicalutamide), gynecomastia and hepatotoxicity. Gynecomastia is on all three anti-androgen lists. Bicalutamide causes the least GI upset, not the most. The three classes don't all block the receptor. Match the pairs: finasteride and dutasteride (5-alpha-reductase); bicalutamide and enzalutamide (receptor); goserelin and leuprolide (GnRH); anastrozole and letrozole (aromatase). Dr. Fasinu wasn't sure of the tablet strengths in class: know which is higher. Important therapeutic effects and adverse effects Each class has its uses and an adverse effect he kept coming back to: hepatotoxicity for testosterone, and thromboembolism for the estrogens, a clot risk the SERMs and aromatase inhibitors share. His opening case asks which hormone to avoid in which patient. Know this Case 1: avoid testosterone in BPH, pregnancy (he called it absolute) and a man with breast cancer; avoid estrogen in breast cancer and after any thromboembolism. Androgen uses: male hypogonadism, some breast tumors in women, anabolic effects, refractory anemia, osteoporosis, growth, and andropause. Testosterone's most important adverse effect is hepatotoxicity: patients are screened, and liver disease rules it out. Also avoid it in pregnancy, heart disease, and prostate or breast cancer in men. Androgen side effects are worse in women and children. Women: hirsutism, a deepened voice, an enlarged clitoris, smaller breasts, sometimes irreversible. Men: sleep apnea, priapism, and gynecomastia, believed to come from testosterone converted to estradiol. Both: acne, edema, jaundice, lower HDL and higher LDL. Testosterone gel or cream: apply it last thing at night, since a hug can pass it through the skin to a child. Estrogen uses: primary hypogonadism, postmenopausal hormone therapy, oral contraceptives, suppressing ovulation in intractable dysmenorrhea or hirsutism, fertility treatment. Thromboembolism is "the most serious and most common side effect of estrogens": they raise clotting factors II, VII, IX and X and lower antithrombin III. Other estrogen side effects. Common: nausea, fluid retention, breakthrough bleeding, breast tenderness. Serious: clots, endometrial and breast cancer, hypertension. Fluid retention is shared by androgens and estrogens and worsens hypertension and heart failure. In menopause therapy, adding progesterone reduces or eliminates estrogen's added uterine cancer risk. Estrogen contraindications: pregnancy, incomplete bone growth, undiagnosed genital bleeding, a stroke or any clot, even 10 years ago, heart disease, a family history of breast or uterine cancer. Estrogens make oral anticoagulants such as warfarin work less well, because they raise clotting factor production. SERMs share the clot risk: raloxifene raises DVT and PE risk 2 to 3 times; tamoxifen raises uterine cancer and clot risk. His Case 5: a woman on raloxifene after an extraction; watch for a clot while she is immobilized. Clomiphene: multiple births and ovarian cysts. Aromatase inhibitors: "at least" remember hot flashes and thromboembolism. Not with hepatic damage or before menopause. Progestins: contraception, dysmenorrhea, endometriosis, precocious puberty; adverse effects hypertension, lower HDL, cancer risk with estrogen. The anti-androgens' side effects are in the item above. Gynecomastia on testosterone comes from estradiol, not DHT. Hirsutism is an androgen side effect, not an estrogen one; preventing DVT is not an estrogen use; BPH is a reason to avoid testosterone, not a use. Estrogen makes warfarin work less well. Raloxifene's dental risk is a clot, not gingival overgrowth, immunosuppression or low calcium. His slide's "thrombolytic complications" means clots forming. For pregnancy, Case 1's answer is testosterone (aloud he said estrogen is used in a few pregnant women; his slide lists pregnancy as an estrogen contraindication). For children the slide says extreme caution and aloud he was firmer; no question depends on it. Key terms GnRH analogs Long-acting copies of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, chiefly goserelin (Zoladex) and leuprolide (Lupron). Natural GnRH is pulsed; the analogs stimulate continuously, so the pituitary switches off and FSH, LH and testosterone fall. Mainly for prostate cancer; side effects are impotence and gynecomastia. progestins Progesterone and its analogs (hydroxyprogesterone, levonorgestrel) that activate the progestin receptor and suppress FSH and LH, preventing ovulation: the progestin-only pill and Plan B (high-dose levonorgestrel, within 72 hours). Adverse effects: hypertension and lower HDL. antiandrogens Drugs that lower androgen activity three ways: GnRH analogs shut down production, 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) stop activation to DHT, and androgen receptor antagonists (flutamide, bicalutamide) block the receptor. Gynecomastia is common to all three. 5α-reductase inhibitors Finasteride (Proscar, higher strength, for BPH; Propecia, lower strength, for hair loss) and dutasteride (Avodart): they block testosterone's conversion to DHT, its active form. Side effects: gynecomastia and sexual dysfunction, like the low libido and breast tenderness of his dental case. L19 · Introduction to Hematology Recognition and major functions of RBCs, platelets, and leukocytes Blood holds three kinds of cells: red cells, platelets and white cells. Know each by its described features (there are no stained images on the exam) and by its job. For the white cells, "we've got two classes and 5 types." Know this Erythrocytes are most of the cells in the blood, about 99 percent, and carry oxygen and carbon dioxide. Platelets are pieces of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, and they initiate blood clotting: "just knowledge you should know." Granulocytes, with prominent granules: neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils. Agranulocytes, without them: monocytes and lymphocytes (B, T and NK cells). Most to least common: neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils (Never Let Monkeys Eat Bananas; the shares are in the table). Lymphocyte sizes: NK cells are the large ones; B and T cells are smaller. Hematopoiesis: one pluripotential stem cell, two lines. The lymphoid line makes the B and T lymphocytes. The myeloid line stays in the marrow and makes the red cells, megakaryocytes (platelets), granulocytes and monocytes. In an adult, every blood cell comes from the bone marrow. Neutrophil 50 to 70% Multi-lobed Two kinds; elastase and myeloperoxidase in the primary ones Lymphocyte 30 to 40% Big, round, slightly indented; thin rim of pale cytoplasm None prominent Monocyte 2 to 8% One, not lobed (indented or horseshoe); a large cell None prominent Eosinophil 1 to 4% Bilobed Large, red with eosin Basophil Under 1% Bilobed Very large, dark blue to purple Watch for: Platelets are made in the bone marrow, not the spleen (the spleen stores about a third of them and clears the old ones). Red cells carry the gases and platelets clot, never the reverse. The monocyte comes from the myeloid line even though it has no prominent granules. Said not needed: the counts per liter in his table ("no reason to memorize the typical concentration of cells") and the colony-forming unit names. Functions of neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils, monocytes, and lymphocytes Each white cell has one main job, and the bank asks it from a description or a raised count: neutrophils for bacteria, eosinophils for parasites and allergy, basophils for histamine and asthma, monocytes for the macrophage they become. Know this Neutrophil: the main phagocyte of the blood and the first line of defense against bacteria; in the blood about 10 hours, then into the tissues. A multi-lobed nucleus, a lot of glycogen, primary granules with elastase and myeloperoxidase, and a second kind with lysozyme and proteases. Eosinophil: peroxidase binds microorganisms and helps kill them; major basic protein (MBP) disrupts the membranes of parasites and makes basophils release histamine. Eosinophils rise in parasitic infections (protozoa, helminths) and in allergic reactions such as hay fever, and carry IgE receptors. Basophil: granules of heparin and vasoactive substances such as histamine, released when IgE binds its IgE receptors; a prominent role in bronchial asthma. Monocyte: in the blood about 3 days, then into the tissues, where it becomes the macrophage (the mononuclear phagocytic system). It phagocytoses bacteria, cells and debris, and its MHC class II presents antigen to helper T cells. Lymphocytes: immunocompetent cells that recognize and respond to antigen: B cells (become antibody-making plasma cells), T cells (help or kill) and NK cells (kill altered cells). Watch for: About 10 hours is the neutrophil; about 3 days is the monocyte. Eosinophils and basophils share a bilobed nucleus and IgE receptors: the granules tell them apart. The monocyte becomes the macrophage, not the plasma cell (that's the B cell), a mast cell or a megakaryocyte. MBP attacks parasites; it is not an Fc receptor (that's the NK cell's CD16). Dr. Dal Zotto said the classification "is going to be simple" for you: germ cell tumors against the rest, and within them, seminoma against the non-seminomatous tumors, because seminoma responds to radiotherapy and the others don't respond as well. Know this Inside the seminiferous tubules: the germ cells (spermatogonia) and the Sertoli cells, which conduct their maturation. Outside: the Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone. Sertoli and Leydig cells are sex cord-stromal cells, not germ cells. 95 percent of testicular tumors are germ cell tumors, from the spermatogonia, and they are cured in more than 95 percent of cases. The rest: sex cord-stromal tumors (Sertoli and Leydig cell tumors) or mixed tumors; in older men, lymphoma involving the testis secondarily, and metastases. The risk factor to know: cryptorchidism. The incidence varies by country (Norway highest) and, unlike penile cancer, is not tied to low socioeconomic status. Seminoma, the most frequent: young adults (30s and 40s); white, multinodular and solid, with no hemorrhage and no necrosis; associated with cryptorchidism. Seminoma usually has no serum tumor marker, so a pathologist makes the diagnosis. It behaves very well and responds to radiotherapy. Non-seminomatous: embryonal carcinoma, yolk sac tumor, choriocarcinoma and teratoma, which recapitulate fetal tissues. More aggressive (choriocarcinoma most of all), and they don't respond as well to radiotherapy. Major benign and malignant prostate disorders The prostate has two big diseases, and where each starts predicts how it behaves. BPH, benign, grows around the urethra, so it blocks the urine; prostatic adenocarcinoma, malignant, starts in the peripheral zone, so it doesn't obstruct early. The cancer is found by PSA, spreads to bone and is graded by Gleason. Know this The prostate: about 20 grams, below the bladder, the urethra running through it. It makes glycoproteins such as PSA (prostate-specific antigen) that keep the sperm nourished and moving. The zones predict the disease: BPH arises around the urethra (the transition, or periurethral, zone); carcinoma in the peripheral zone, toward the back. BPH: hyperplasia of both the glands and the stroma, in nearly every man after 50 ("you cannot avoid this"); it obstructs the urethra, so urinating is hard. Hormones play a role; surgery treats severe obstruction. It wasn't taught as a precursor of carcinoma. Prostatic adenocarcinoma: the most frequent cancer in men, in men over 65; from the peripheral zone, it doesn't obstruct early. It is found by serum PSA, a simple blood draw: its glands make much more PSA than normal ones (the lecture said 10 times). It "likes the bones": its bone metastases form bone (osteoblastic). An osteoblastic lesion in a man means: think prostate, order a PSA. Gleason grading grades differentiation, from well-differentiated glands to masses of tumor and single cells; the worse the differentiation, the worse the prognosis. Its tumors: VaIN and squamous cell carcinoma (reproductive age), and sarcoma botryoides (girls under 5). Lichen simplex chronicus: vulvar skin thickened and leathery (hyperkeratosis, hypergranulosis, acanthosis) from continuous scratching and rubbing, a reaction to anything that itches. Lichen sclerosus: unknown cause (postulated autoimmune). A completely atrophic epithelium over dermal sclerosis and hyalinization; the vulva looks smooth, like parchment paper. It itches, so lichen simplex chronicus can form on top. Lichen sclerosus is "the single non-infectious inflammatory disorder that can lead to carcinomas": the HPV-independent vulvar squamous cell carcinoma of women over 60. Diagnose and treat it in time. Distinguishing neoplastic from non-neoplastic lesions Sort each lesion by what it is: inflammation and infection are non-neoplastic; a proliferation of abnormal cells (an intraepithelial neoplasia, a carcinoma, a sarcoma) is neoplastic. Neither word settles the risk alone: an inflammatory lichen can lead to cancer, and a neoplastic lesion stays in situ until it invades the stroma. Know this Non-neoplastic: vaginitis (Candida, Trichomonas, atrophic), the vulva's lichen simplex chronicus, lichen sclerosus and lichen planus, and the inflamed transformation zone. In situ lesions are confined to the epithelium; once one invades the stroma, it is squamous cell carcinoma. Non-neoplastic isn't always harmless: lichen sclerosus is inflammatory but predisposes to carcinoma. And condyloma acuminatum (HPV 6 and 11) is benign, not premalignant. Relationship between HPV and cervical neoplasia Cervical cancer starts where the cervix's two linings meet, the transformation zone, because their constant "fight" keeps it inflamed and open to HPV. High-risk HPV causes the precursor lesions, which the Pap test finds by their koilocytes, so screening and the vaccine can prevent the cancer. Know this Endocervix: mucinous glandular (columnar), red. Ectocervix: non-keratinizing squamous, white. The transformation zone is their junction, where the epithelia collide, "the fighting of epithelia." It is constantly inflamed and injured, so open to infection, above all HPV, and it is where cervical cancer arises. The precursors: squamous intraepithelial lesions (SIL; CIN). Low grade progress slowly and can regress; high grade are less likely to regress and more likely to progress. About 90 percent are linked to HPV, in the reproductive years; the high-risk types are 16 and 18. The koilocyte, HPV's cytopathic effect: a bigger nucleus with a clear halo around it (a true cavity). Cytology looks for it in a Pap smear; biopsies show it too. High grade: crowding, hyperchromasia, loss of maturation; in cytology, less cytoplasm, a higher nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio and pleomorphic nuclei. SILs are in situ; once they invade the stroma, they are squamous cell carcinoma. Cervical cancer is fourth in women worldwide (breast is first), less frequent in the United States thanks to Pap screening, which lowers incidence and mortality; about a fourth of U.S. women lack access. The HPV vaccine lowers the incidence, especially in adolescents, but its full benefit may take decades. Management is now risk-based.
